blocks.text: Yet since the species of flies and gnats are innumerable, it is not clear which in particular ذباب [dhubāb], זבוב designates. Perhaps it is a general name, comprehending all those insects which the Latins include under the name of muscae [flies] and culices [gnats]: for example, the gnat of Egypt, with white joints, the size of the common gnat, of a dusky grey colour; the fly of the Buphthalmum, common in Egypt, smaller in size than the common bee, with four wings, short, club-shaped antennae stretched forward and bearing a bristle on the back, an oblong, convex, shining, dark green thorax, and six legs on the thorax. These two insects were carefully described by Hasselquist, in his Travels p. 470. 471. German trans. Further, the troublesome gnat of Forsskål (in Descript. Animall. p. 85), in size and appearance like the common piping gnat, hairy over the whole body and the legs, with bristle-like antennae and dusky wings, which is found in immense numbers at Rosetta, Cairo and Alexandria, is a nuisance to sleepers at night, and can scarcely be kept off except by a well-closed curtain. Finally, the black fly also seems to belong here, with bristle-like antennae and a thorax with yellow spots, which Forsskål briefly lists among the insects of Arabia observed by him, p. 24. Eugène Roger, in his Description of Palestine, written in French (La Terre Sainte, Paris, 1664, 4to), p. 84, mentions small black flies called Bargaches (the sound of the word is to be rendered with French pronunciation, for it is the Arabic بَرْغَشْ [barghash], the same as بَعُوضْ [baʿūḍ], gnat, or a certain species of gnats, in Golius p. 259), whose swarms, borne in like dense clouds, attacked the camp of the Arabs with such violence that men and animals were almost deprived of the ability to breathe. And Oedmann, in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 4, ch. 9, p. 81 ff., thought it credible that the same species of flies is denoted by the Hebrew זבוב, chiefly on account of the passage Es. VII, 18, where the incredible multitude of Egyptians who would invade the territory of Israel is set forth under the image of flies called זבוב. But in fasc. 6, ch. 9, p. 79, he himself changed his opinion, understanding it of that species of gadfly or oestrus which Bruce, who often saw it in Ethiopia, described at length in his Travels vol. 5, p. 190 ff. of Volkmann's German trans., where you will also find a picture of this insect, plate 39. The Ethiopians call it Tsaltsalia. This species of oestrus was unknown to Linnaeus. But Gmelin, in the Notes on Bruce's Travels edited by Hassencamp, p. 31, thinks it should be designated by the name oestrus fusco-pilosus, alis immaculatis. Compare, however, what Blumenbach remarked on Bruce's description of this insect, vol. 5, p. 291 f. German trans. Oedmann, however, considers that oestrus to be the זבוב of the Hebrews, moved by no other reason than that he thinks it more suitable to the passage Esaiah VII, 14 than that black fly which Roger described loc. cit. [III, 343] How uncertain this argument is, everyone will see for himself. With the same right, and perhaps greater, he could have referred here some species of the flies which we mentioned above from Hasselquist and Forsskål. It will be safest to regard זבוב, like the Arabic ذباب [dhubāb] and the Syriac ܕܒܒܐ?, as a general name for various species of flies and gnats.
